item: The v11.6 live register (`docs/blueprint/traceability-matrix.md`) shows 0% complete and every one of 1566 requirements as UNASSESSED, even though a full assessment pass covering all 1566 requirements already exists in `docs/blueprint/assessment/*.json` (60 files, untracked in git) — and the acceptance suite's own staleness check fails on exactly this file right now
files: docs/blueprint/assessment/CICD-b1.json (1 of 60 untracked files; git status shows the whole directory as `??`)
backend/crates/apps/qip-cli/src/blueprint.rs:6-20 (module doc: three sources, three rendered views)
why: ADR 0099 makes this matrix the structural, must-not-be-hand-edited live register for the whole v11.6 programme, generated by `qip blueprint render` from `docs/blueprint/assessment/*.json`. That assessment work has actually been done — 60 domain files totalling exactly 1566 rows (134 COMPLETE, 557 PARTIAL, 629 MISSING, 177 BLOCKED, 42 NEEDS-VALIDATION, 20 INCORRECT, 7 OBSOLETE) — but the files are untracked and the committed matrix predates them (matrix mtime 1790366225 vs. assessment mtimes from 1790366334 onward), so it still reads 0%/UNASSESSED everywhere. Running the acceptance suite's own guard confirms this is a present, not hypothetical, defect: `cargo test -p qip-acceptance --test documentation the_blueprint_views_are_what_their_sources_render_to` FAILED in this exact checkout with `these blueprint views differ from what their sources render to: ["docs/blueprint/traceability-matrix.md"]`. Anyone reading the register that ADR 0099 says to trust structurally is currently told the programme is at 0%, which is a false statement about the state of the system by the enterprise-governance rule's own definition. The fix is mechanical and already built (`qip blueprint render`) — what is missing is committing the assessment JSON and re-running the render as part of the workflow, not new code.

item: The GitOps control plane (Argo CD + Config Connector on GKE Autopilot, ADR 0036) has never successfully bootstrapped in any environment: `vendor.yml`'s blocking Trivy gate refuses Argo CD's image on CVE-2025-68121 with no fixed upstream kustomize/git-lfs available, which also blocks cert-manager's images in the same fail-fast mirror loop, and `infra.yml`'s `up` action cannot complete a working control plane as a result
files: .github/workflows/vendor.yml:353 (module comment: CVE-2025-68121 lives in two third-party binaries Argo CD downloads)
docs/DELIVERY-STATUS.md:244 ("Argo CD fails the scan gate" row, measured against v3.5.3/v3.6.0-rc1 and upstream kustomize v5.8.1)
docs/adr/0093-*.md (dev cluster suspended as the recorded consequence)
why: DELIVERY-STATUS.md's own measurement (not a release note) shows there is no newer kustomize to adopt — v5.8.1, the version Argo CD already ships, is upstream's latest as of 2026-02-09 — and the RC build still carries the vulnerable binary on an old Go toolchain, so this cannot be cleared by bumping a version. It explicitly instructs: do not clear with a scanner exception, a .trivyignore, or a per-image acknowledgement. The only two paths forward are (a) an upstream Argo CD release that actually fixes the CVE, which nothing in this repository can produce, or (b) the owner deciding ADR 0099's open conflict C3 (whether the platform keeps GKE/Argo CD at all, versus the Cloud Run-only direction v2.1 also allows). Until one of those exists, every ADR-0036-governed warm-service GitOps path stays unusable in every environment, which is exactly why this is a needs-evidence item rather than something an agent can refactor or replace unilaterally.

item: Twelve non-Rust delivery-tooling files (eight Python, four Node) exist under `.claude/hooks/` and `scripts/`, with no ADR recording the deviation from the platform's "Rust everywhere" rule — the acceptance suite pins the set as accepted rather than arguing for it, and one of the twelve, `terraform-undeletable.py`, is load-bearing on the infrastructure pipeline itself
files: backend/crates/tests/qip-acceptance/tests/blueprint_rules.rs:148 ("the deviation is real, no ADR records it")
.github/workflows/infra.yml:569 (reclaim what the teardown left standing, calls terraform-undeletable.py)
why: ADR 0001/0011 and v11.6's own §2 Non-Negotiable Architecture Rules (rule 1's tooling clause, per the test's own comment) commit to Rust everywhere with the browser as the sole named exception; delivery tooling is a second, unrecorded exception the tree already carries. This is not hypothetical drift — the very next commit in this repository's history (3b48f91b) shows a thirteenth Python file landing and being caught only because a later, unrelated commit ran the full acceptance suite instead of the narrower suite the change looked like it touched; had that gate lapse not been repaired, the deviation would have grown silently again. Fixing the twelve that remain the way the renderer was fixed (migrate into `qip-cli`, which already proved it can do JSON-in/Markdown-out work with only `serde_json`) is possible for some of them, but not obviously right for all — `terraform-undeletable.py` runs inside `infra.yml` itself and a browser-automation job (`venue-signup/`) is explicitly walled off from the platform's own dependency graph by design. The decision needed is which of the twelve get an ADR carve-out and which get migrated, not a unilateral rewrite.

item: `deploy.yml`'s execution-node rolling-replace step and `image.yml`'s boot-image bake have never run in any environment — `execution_nodes = {}` in every environment's tfvars — leaving ADR 0035's one authorised node (dev, `newyork-1`, shadow mode) unbuilt pending three sequenced human acts none of which any workflow performs on its own
files: .github/workflows/deploy.yml:585-592,739-765 (replace every execution node under its group's rolling policy — documented no-op)
.github/workflows/image.yml:101-110 (manual-dispatch-only bake, ADR 0035 reference in its own input description)
infrastructure/environments/dev/terraform.tfvars:1-27 (execution_nodes = {} — "a working configuration, not an incomplete one", names the exact blocked sequence)
why: This is not silently broken: deploy.yml's own step detects the empty group and prints "no execution node group exists in ${TARGET_ENVIRONMENT}; nothing to replace" rather than failing, and dev's tfvars carries a five-line comment naming exactly what is missing — a capital-allocation number ADR 0045 proposes but does not set, and a three-step human sequence (uncomment the image-bake subnet CIDR, dispatch infra.yml action=up, only then dispatch image.yml) where doing it out of order refuses by design. The evidence needed before this can move to B or be scored differently is simply that the sequence has been run: an image self-link written into dev's tfvars and a capital number chosen. Nothing here is a defect to refactor; it is a deliberately incomplete migration waiting on two decisions no workflow may make.

item: `Makefile`'s `test` target omits `--no-fail-fast`, unlike `ci.yml`'s test job, the Makefile's own `count` target, and CLAUDE.md's documented command — a local `make test` can abort at the first failing binary and under-report, which is the exact failure mode this repository's own rules call out by name
files: .claude/rules/02-change-management.md ("Use --no-fail-fast... a run that reports 64 passing tests out of 3,075 looks like a small suite rather than an aborted one")
why: `.claude/rules/02-change-management.md`, the working agreement every agent in this repository reads first, states this exact risk in these exact words as the reason `--no-fail-fast` is mandatory. `make test` is the one place in the tree that does not follow its own rule: a developer or agent running `make test` locally (as opposed to `make count` or CI) gets a build that can stop at the first failing crate and silently describe a fraction of the suite as if it were the whole of it. This is a one-line fix with no design question attached.
blueprint_refs: CICD-049 (GCP v2.1 §14.2 step 3 — Rust builds pass the deny, audit, lint, test, replay and benchmark gates)

item: The two-dependency allowlist exists twice, independently hand-maintained: `scripts/check-dependencies.sh`'s PERMITTED bash array and `backend/deny.toml`'s `[bans].allow` list, kept in agreement only by discipline and by docs/DELIVERY-STATUS.md prose, not by a shared source
why: The two lists currently agree entry-for-entry (verified: both name serde, serde_json, serde_derive, proc-macro2, quote, syn, unicode-ident, serde_core, itoa, zmij, memchr), but they are two independent enumerations of the same fact — exactly the pattern principle 6 of the top-level CLAUDE.md warns about ("two independent claims about the same fact will disagree, and the louder one will be wrong"). A future dependency change edited in one file and not the other would pass one gate and fail the other, or worse, pass both if edited inconsistently under time pressure with nobody noticing the second file exists. Generating one from the other (deny.toml as the single source, with check-dependencies.sh reading it, or vice versa) removes the duplication without removing either gate.

item: `.claude/rules/01-security-and-safety.md` names the destructive-command guard hook `guard-dangerous-command.sh`; the real, current implementation — wired in `.claude/settings.json` and actually executed on every Bash call — is `guard-dangerous-command.py`, a rewrite that fixed a shell-quoting bug the old `.sh` version had
why: The rule this file states is "If the guard fires, do not route around it" — which depends on a reader (human or agent) being able to find and reason about the actual guard. A reader who greps for guard-dangerous-command.sh as this rules file instructs finds nothing, because the file was rewritten in Python specifically to fix a quoting bug the shell version had. The behaviour is correct and enforced; only the documentation's name for it is stale. One-line fix, no design question.

item: Delivery-side regression and audit tooling that exists specifically to catch governance/security regressions is not wired into any CI job or Makefile target: `test_hooks.py` (the destructive-command guard's own regression suite, 17 table-driven cases), `audit-dead-code.py`, and `audit-register.py` (the tool that catches stale evidence claims like the ones this very report was asked to distrust)
why: `test_hooks.py` is the only thing that proves the destructive-command guard still blocks what it claims to block and still allows what it claims to allow ("a guard that refuses everything is not secure, it is broken", per its own docstring) — a guard this important having its regression suite run only by hand means a future edit to the guard can silently stop catching what it exists to catch, with nothing red in CI to say so. The two audit scripts are lower-stakes (advisory, not safety-critical) but exist for the same reason this task exists: to catch drift between what the tree claims and what it does. None of the three needs new code; each needs one job step.

item: No branch-protection or required-review configuration exists anywhere in the tracked tree — no CODEOWNERS file, no `hashicorp/github` Terraform provider, no ruleset — so nothing in the repository can prove or refute whether `main` actually requires status checks or independent review before merge
files: (negative evidence, independently confirmed: `find . -iname CODEOWNERS` and `grep -rn 'provider "github"' infrastructure/` both return nothing)
backend/crates/tests/qip-acceptance/tests/infrastructure.rs:4724-4743 (production_is_never_deployed_automatically — asserts only that a GitHub environment: name exists, not that it requires review)
.github/workflows/deploy.yml:598 (the named GitHub environment: per job, where required reviewers would attach if configured)
why: This is a case the acceptance suite itself cannot close: branch protection is a GitHub repository setting, not repository content, so no test over the tree can assert it either way (docs/blueprint/assessment/CICD-b2.json scores this row NEEDS-VALIDATION for exactly this reason). Before this becomes a B (encode it as a `hashicorp/github` Terraform resource) or is scored A (already configured out-of-band), someone needs to run `gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/main/protection` against the live repository and read the answer — an agent cannot infer it from files.

item: ADR number 0097 has been claimed since 2026-09-21 (four days as of this report) with no body written — the README row describes a real, apparently-unimplemented control (a cell's resting order leg re-measured against its own path-5 check on every pass it waits, withdrawn once the spread it earns stops covering the concession a sweep would extract) but nothing decides or implements it, and the number is deliberately left unlinked
files: docs/adr/README.md:137 ("Number claimed 2026-09-21; body to follow, and the number is deliberately not a link")
why: `.claude/rules/architecture/00-boundaries.md` documents a real incident on 2026-09-14 where six parallel lanes each read the ADR register, each found the same highest number, and each claimed it — six collisions that took a day to renumber across 74 files. A number claimed and left unwritten for days is exactly the state that makes a second, unrelated claim of the same number-adjacent risk more likely, and it also means whatever behaviour 0097 was going to decide (the resting-leg withdrawal rule) is currently undecided rather than merely undocumented. What is needed is not code: it is confirmation from whoever claimed 0097 that the decision is still live (and a timeline for the body) or a decision to release the number.

item: `ci.yml`'s `secrets` job checks out the full git history (`fetch-depth: 0`), which is unusual among the workflow's jobs (every other checkout is a shallow default), while both the job's own comment and `check-secrets.sh` state the design is deliberately diff-only and never scans history
files: .github/workflows/ci.yml:390-400 (job comment: "The secrets check runs on the diff, not the history"; then `fetch-depth: 0` two lines later)
scripts/check-secrets.sh:1-8 (git grep over the working tree only, no history walk)
why: The comment immediately above the checkout step explains, correctly, why the design does not scan history ("a secret already committed needs rotating rather than a failing build"), which makes the `fetch-depth: 0` two lines below it read as a contradiction to a reader who has not traced through to check-secrets.sh's implementation — and it buys nothing: the script only ever greps the checked-out working tree, so a shallow checkout would produce an identical result at lower cost on every push. Low-impact, but it is exactly the kind of self-contradicting configuration the codebase's own "say why" principle exists to prevent.

item: The worker-orchestration concurrency ladder (8/16/32/64/100, gated on a measured ≥10% improvement in verified output per token) and the model-gateway's call-budget/pause mechanism are self-measured by policy convention and exercised by hand — no automated check enforces that a rung only climbs on real measurement, or that work queued beyond the current ceiling is refused rather than silently over-subscribed
files: docs/plan/algorik-orchestration-policy.md:58-83 (the ladder and its climb/drop rules, stated as policy prose)
scripts/worker-capacity.sh:1-30 (reports the ceiling; does not gate anything, always exits 0)
scripts/model-gateway.test.mjs (covers configure/probe/screenPayload/completionText; the exhaustion/refusal path in run() has no named test)
why: `worker-capacity.sh`'s own purpose statement is explicit that it reports rather than gates, and ADR 0098 records the ladder as a policy the desktop-fabric programme runs by, not as something any tool enforces. That is a reasonable shape for a human-supervised ladder, but it means the two failure modes the ladder exists to prevent — climbing a rung on noise rather than a measured improvement, and over-subscribing workers past the ceiling worker-capacity.sh actually measured — are both currently unguarded by anything that would turn red. The gateway side of this is closer to done than the ladder side: model-gateway.mjs already fails closed on a missing budget config; what is missing is a test proving run() actually refuses once ALGORIK_WORKER_MAX_CALLS is exhausted.
